label: post-guard batch — verified fresh against live tiers, exponents/logs/angles/functions

widget.prompt: 16^(1/2) asks for a square root. Reframe it forward: find the base whose SQUARE is 16.
widget.successFeedback: Base 4, so 4² = 16 — and that is exactly what 16^(1/2) = 4 means, read the other way. Raising to the 1/2 power and squaring undo each other, so the two questions are the same question asked from opposite ends.

widget.prompt: Slide the base until base^(2/3) reads 4.
widget.successFeedback: Base 8: 8^(2/3) = (8^(1/3))² = 2² = 4. The fractional exponent does two jobs at once — the denominator (3) roots, the numerator (2) then powers — and both happen to this one base.

widget.prompt: First find the POSITIVE case: slide the base until base^(1/3) reads 2.
widget.successFeedback: Base 8 gives 8^(1/3) = 2. Now apply the negative sign the question actually asked: a negative exponent means take the reciprocal, so 8^(−1/3) = 1/2 — the widget verifies the root, the sign flips it afterward.

widget.prompt: 3 · 2ˣ = 24 divides down to 2ˣ = 8 first. Slide the base until base³ reads 8.
widget.successFeedback: Base 2, and 2³ = 8, so x = 3. The leading 3 is not part of the exponential — it is a coefficient that has to be cleared by division BEFORE the base-matching even starts.

widget.prompt: (1/2)ˣ = 1/8. Slide the base to 0.5 and watch where x = 3 lands.
widget.successFeedback: (1/2)³ = 1/8 — a base below 1 shrinks as the exponent grows, which is why decay problems and "a half raised to a power" always move the same direction.

widget.prompt: A = 200·e^(0.05·20) = 200·e¹. e is not a round number, so slide the base until b¹ lands near 2.7 — the finest step this dial reaches.
widget.successFeedback: This dial's best step is 2.7; e itself is 2.71828…, close enough that the two agree to two places. Using the lesson's own e ≈ 2.718, the growth factor is 200 × 2.718 ≈ 544 — the widget shows WHY the number lands near 2.7-and-a-bit, without pretending a dial in tenths can reach an irrational number exactly.
widget.lowFeedback: Still below e — the growth factor has not caught up to 2.7 yet.
widget.highFeedback: Past e now — the dial has gone beyond 2.7.

widget.prompt: 15 hours is three 5-hour half-lives. Slide the base to 0.5 and read base³.
widget.successFeedback: (1/2)³ = 0.125, and 240 × 0.125 = 30 mg. Counting half-lives is counting how many times the base multiplies in — three halvings, not a division by three.

widget.prompt: One angle of a linear pair is fixed at 50°. Drag the other angle until the pair completes a straight line.
widget.successFeedback: 130°, since 50 + 130 = 180. A linear pair always fills a straight angle — that is what the name means — so knowing one angle hands you the other by subtraction, every time.
widget.lowFeedback: Not there yet — the two angles do not yet total 180°.
widget.highFeedback: Past 130° — the pair now totals more than a straight line.

widget.prompt: ∠AOC is a straight angle. Ray OB sits inside it with ∠AOB fixed at 116°. Drag ∠BOC until the two pieces complete the straight angle.
widget.successFeedback: 64°, since 116 + 64 = 180. An interior ray splits a straight angle into two pieces that always add back to 180 — the same linear-pair fact, just with a ray drawn instead of two full angles.
widget.lowFeedback: The two pieces do not yet total 180°.
widget.highFeedback: The two pieces now total more than 180°.

widget.prompt: Trace y = x³ to x = 2 and read the height.
widget.successFeedback: y = 8, since 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. A cube is three copies multiplied, not three copies added — the trace shows the curve climbing far faster than a straight line as x grows, which is the visual signature of that difference.
widget.lowFeedback: Still to the left of x = 2.

widget.prompt: f⁻¹(11) is the y for which f(y) = 11. Since f(x) = 3x − 4, that means 3y − 4 = 11. Clear the units, then split.
widget.successFeedback: y = 5, so f⁻¹(11) = 5 — and checking it the OTHER way, f(5) = 3(5) − 4 = 11 confirms it. Evaluating an inverse and solving the original equation are the same question; f⁻¹(x) = (x+4)/3 is just this same solving process done once and for all.
widget.unbalancedFeedback: The pans disagree — the same operation must hit both sides.
widget.notIsolatedFeedback: y is not alone yet — units remain on its pan.
widget.missFeedback: Not the solution. Add the 4 units back to both pans first, then split into 3 groups.
widget.unexpandedFeedback: Deal with the units before splitting into groups.

refusals.title: Conjecture vs proof, two-column proof, transversal angle family, converses
refusals.why: Classification and proof-structure lessons — sort a statement as conjecture or proof, match a statement to its justifying reason, sort angle pairs, judge whether a converse holds. The thing being manipulated would have to be the reasoning itself. cp-05-01's numeric alternate-interior-angle step was also checked: no transversal/parallel-line engine exists in the catalogue (verified by search — zero matches for Transversal or ParallelLine in schema.ts). Refused.

refusals.title: Notation, rotations as functions, rotational symmetry, congruence defined, corresponding parts
refusals.why: gf-01-03 and gf-05-03 are classification/matching, no engine. gf-03-03, gf-04-03 and gf-05-01 all need ROTATION as manipulable state — checked transformExplore's full schema directly: it has shape, target, gridMin/Max, dxMin/Max, dyMin/Max, allowReflect. NO rotation field of any kind. Translation and reflection are modelled; rotation is not. This is a genuine engine gap, not a fit failure — the same shape as the radical-simplification and parametric-motion gaps already found. A rotation-capable engine (or an allowRotate extension to transformExplore) would convert these three plus likely more corpus-wide. Refused pending that decision.

refusals.title: Mixed operations & restrictions, LCD, unlike denominators, horizontal asymptotes, inverse & joint variation
refusals.why: rf-03-02/03 and rf-04-03 confirmed again (symbolic LCD; asymptote-type classification). rf-02-03 counts excluded domain values symbolically — no engine. rf-05-03 (inverse variation) was checked against proportionalReasoningLab's full task enum: unitRate | bestRate | predictOutput | predictInput | steadyAssumption | testProportional | constant | scaleRatio | percentOf | discount | cheaperThenPredict. Every task models y = kx (direct variation, constant RATIO); none models xy = k (constant PRODUCT). Forcing 'constant' onto an inverse relationship would compute the wrong invariant. Refused.

refusals.title: Circumcenter & incenter, centroid & orthocenter, choosing the right center
refusals.why: Confirmed again: no engine represents a triangle centre or the concurrency of bisectors/medians/altitudes. This remains the triangleCentreLab build candidate (3 lessons here). Refused.

refusals.title: Inequalities in Proofs
refusals.why: RE-EXAMINED with the actual algebra, not a numeric-fit attempt. The exterior angle theorem (E = R1 + R2) is a linear relationship among the triangle's OWN angles, but triangleAngleLab's 180-degree total is fixed by the geometry of a real drawn triangle with two FIXED corners — it cannot be repointed to sum to an arbitrary E without reverse-engineering coordinates that fix a second angle at a chosen value, which the engine's interface does not expose. Distinct from S203N's vague 'clean-number check failed': this is a structural mismatch between what the theorem needs (three related but independently nameable angles) and what the engine offers (one dragged angle plus a fixed 180 total). Refused.

refusals.title: Logarithmic Scales
refusals.why: DISCOVERED BY THE SOLVABILITY GATE, not by inspection. expLogExplore's base is bounded [0.2, 10] with NO room above 10 — startBase shares the same ceiling, so nothing can approach the target from above. Richter/decibel scaling needs base EXACTLY 10 (a defined constant, not an approximable limit like e), so unlike lg-05-01 there is no honest nearby grid point to substitute -- 9.9 would misrepresent a scale that is, by definition, exactly base 10. Refused: a genuine engine ceiling, not a fit failure.
